disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus, organizing tasks, and following through on activities, that leads to clinically significant impairment in functioning for at least six months across settings. Hyperactivity and impulsivity are minimal or absent, distinguishing this presentation from combined or hyperactive-impulsive types. In adults, it often presents as disorganization, mental fatigue with sustained tasks, and chronic inefficiency rather than overt behavioral problems seen in childhood. It must be differentiated from cognitive decline, mood or anxiety disorders, and the effects of medical illness or substances; in adults, symptoms often become more apparent or impairing when life demands for self-management and multitasking increase.

narrative.personality: Allan is routine-driven, community-minded, and compassionate, taking pride in being dependable and hands-on both at work and in his family life.
narrative.stressor: Over the past couple of years, Allan’s venue shifted from predictable local events to a busier schedule with more complex ticketing systems, rotating crews, and frequent last-minute changes, placing heavier demands on planning and coordination than he was used to. As the calendar filled with overlapping shifts, safety briefings, and cash reports, he found it increasingly hard to keep track of what needed to be done next once he stepped away from his written checklist, and small oversights began to affect both his team and the guest experience. At the same time, his responsibilities at home expanded as he tried to help aging parents while maintaining his volunteer work and family traditions, stretching his capacity to juggle many modest but time-sensitive tasks across the week. After nearly a year of missed callbacks, overlooked errands, and a few pointed comments from his supervisor about lapses in follow-through, his wife urged him to seek an evaluation when he confessed that keeping up with everyday obligations now felt like an exhausting, confusing slog rather than the steady routine he once enjoyed.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m getting tired of promising I’ll do simple things and then realizing I completely forgot about them.”

narrative.personality: Edward is reserved, intellectually curious, and methodical, with a practical streak and a quiet pride in being well-prepared and reliable.
narrative.stressor: As Edward began transitioning from a fast-paced advisory role into a semi-retired 'legacy consulting' arrangement, his days shifted from a tightly structured schedule to a patchwork of part-time client work, museum volunteering, and personal projects. Without the external scaffolding of a traditional workday and an assistant to organize his materials, he found himself setting up new home-based systems for files, devices, and reference books, only to realize he couldn’t reliably keep track of where things were or what he had planned for the afternoon. The freedom of this new phase of life accentuated long-standing but previously compensated tendencies toward mental drifting when he moved between tasks, which now interfered with simple routines like preparing for a docent tour or a client call. After several episodes of misplacing items he considered essential to his identity—like his favorite annotated market texts and his volunteer badge—and feeling uncharacteristically embarrassed in front of clients and museum staff, he agreed with his wife’s suggestion to consult a psychiatrist to understand why everyday organization had become such an unexpected struggle.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep misplacing the things I need for my day, and it’s starting to interfere with my work and volunteering.”

narrative.personality: Jacob is quiet, detail-oriented, and self-reliant, preferring structured, solitary work and hobbies where he can focus deeply without distraction.
narrative.stressor: About a year ago, Jacob’s company pushed more adjusters into remote and hybrid work with heavier caseloads, expecting them to self-manage scheduling, documentation, and client communication with minimal administrative support. Initially, he welcomed the solitude, but as the volume of small, time-bound tasks increased—follow-up calls, virtual inspections, status updates—he began to feel overwhelmed by the constant need to remember what needed to be done after each interaction without the external structure of an office. His longstanding habit of focusing intensely on a single file or project now worked against him, as he would emerge from deep work to realize he had neglected routine obligations at home and work, leading to strained conversations with his spouse, delayed payments, and warnings from his manager about missed deadlines. After nearly a year of living in what he described to his wife as a perpetual state of being 'behind on the basics' despite working harder than ever, he sought psychiatric help hoping to understand why keeping up with ordinary responsibilities had become so difficult.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep meaning to take care of basic things—bills, calls, appointments—and then realizing I’ve completely let them slip.”
